1.pericope_label: Come thou into the ark: the invitation and the commendation

schools.summary: Gill places the word seven days before the flood, the ark built and everything ready. Calvin measures what the command cost: Noah had sustained a hundred years of the fiercest assaults, but the severest contest was to bid farewell to the world, renounce society and bury himself in the ark — and the timing made it harder, the face of the earth being lovely just then, in the season when herbs shoot and trees flourish, God choosing the very spring to destroy the world. It was no light trial to leave the only life he had known for six hundred years and live in a sepulchre he had spent a century digging for himself, with nothing to confirm the warning, men all around him feasting and building sumptuous houses. On the commendation Calvin sees a difficulty and will not pass it by: if Noah was saved because he was righteous, it seems to follow that we may deserve life by works. His answers are that the design was to set one man against the whole world, so that in his person the unrighteousness of all might be condemned; and that accepting a man's righteousness is not repugnant to free acceptance, since God accepts gifts he himself conferred, loving men freely, adopting them in Christ, justifying them by mercy, and only then regenerating them — from which good works flow afterwards, not before.

Henry fastens on the wording and gets the best of the chapter from it. God does not bid Noah go into the ark but come into it, implying that God would go with him, lead him in, keep him company, and in due time bring him out; and that presence made the ark — a prison in itself — not merely a refuge but a palace. He notes too that Noah did not enter until bidden, though he knew what the vessel was for. On the household he will not tidy away what the invitation involved: one son was Ham, who proved a bad man and was yet saved, whence he draws that wicked children often fare better for godly parents' sake, and that there is a mixture of bad with good in the best societies — in Noah's family a Ham, in Christ's a Judas. Henry and Wesley then define the righteousness in nearly identical words: those are righteous indeed who are righteous before God, having not only the form of godliness, by which they appear righteous to men easily imposed upon, but the power of it, by which they approve themselves to God who searches the heart. Henry adds that in a world of wicked people God could see one righteous Noah — that grain of wheat could not be lost, not in so great a heap of chaff.
Wesley states the definition of righteousness with Henry, almost word for word, marking the difference between the form of godliness and its power.

Ellicott fills in what the week was for — the building over, the remaining days spent collecting the animals — and corrects a common misreading: many suppose a hundred and twenty years were spent on the work, but that rests on an untenable reading of an earlier verse which really fixes the duration of human life.

outliers.note: insists the hardest part of the command was its timing, spring having just come and the doomed world never looking better

themes: come, not go

2.pericope_label: Clean and unclean before the law, and the seven days' reprieve

schools.summary: Gill infers the distinction of clean and unclean was known before the flood, grounding it in the practice of sacrificing ever since the fall, men having been taught by revelation both to sacrifice and what to offer. On the delay he reports three explanations — mourning for Methuselah, an addition to the years granted for repentance, or simply time for Noah to settle his family and the creatures — and prefers the last. Calvin, on the repeated command, holds it no bare repetition but a commendation of Noah's uniform obedience: in whatever particular it pleased God to try him he remained constant, since it is not becoming to obey one commandment only and then feel free to withdraw. On the number he makes it three pairs with a single animal added for sacrifice, noting that Le Clerc objected and supposed seven of each sex.
Henry marks the obedience that answers the command: Noah went in on notice, though no cloud threatened and all was serene, walking at every step by faith and not by sense.

Clarke says the distinction marked which animals were proper for sacrifice and food, suggests the word was spoken on a sabbath, and follows the forty days forward — the period became sacred and proper for humiliation, in the fasts of Moses and Elijah and our Lord, in the respite given to Nineveh, and at length in Lent. Wesley turns the delay into a warning: God granted a reprieve of seven days more, to show how slow he is to anger, but it was all in vain and those days were trifled away like the rest. Noah had told them of judgment at a distance and they put off repenting; now he must tell them it is at the door — and it is common, Wesley adds, for men careless of their souls through years of health, when death looked far off, to be as careless through the seven days of their sickness, when they see it approaching.

Ellicott is careful about what the distinction cannot mean: there can be no reference to the Levitical law, which had respect to human food, nor to a division between tame and wild, since all alike are called cattle; the clean were probably those which from Adam and Abel had been offered in sacrifice. He thinks seven of each kind rather than seven pairs, arguing that otherwise few species could have been included, since attending to so large a number would have been beyond Noah and his sons. He alone raises the documentary question and handles it evenly: these fuller orders are given in the name of Jehovah where most of the narrative is Elohistic, from which some assume a Jehovist completed an earlier account — but the sacrifice is as integral to the Chaldean Genesis as the sending forth of the birds, and so indubitably older than Moses. Yet he concedes there is nothing improbable in Moses having had two records before him, and at least a prima facie appearance of two narratives combined here. Keil agrees the seven means three pair and a single one, probably a male for sacrifice, and denies the distinction proves different authorship. Ellicott also makes the forty days the sacred number of trial and patience, the length of the fast in the wilderness and of the sojourn after the Resurrection.

6.pericope_label: Six hundred years old, and the beasts that came of themselves

schools.summary: Gill works out the arithmetic, that Noah was six hundred when the flood began and in his six hundred and first year when it ended, his eldest son by then a hundred; and on the gathering he allows two explanations, that the creatures came impressed with an instinct from God, or by the ministry of angels. Calvin thinks the age repeated for a reason: old age makes men more indolent and morose, so Noah's faith is the more conspicuous for not failing at that period, and his promptitude deserves its own commendation. He guards the phrase that Noah entered because of the waters — it does not mean he was driven in by their rush, but that being moved by the word he perceived through faith a deluge everyone else was ridiculing. On the animals he meets the charge of absurdity by looking back to the creation: every kind once presented itself to Adam to be named, and we dread wild beasts only because, having shaken off God's yoke, we have lost the authority Adam had. What happened here was a restoration of that state, untamed creatures kept in the ark much as hens and geese are kept in a coop. It was humanly impossible that such an assemblage be made in a moment; but because Noah trusted the outcome to God, God gave power to his own precept, so that Noah's faith availed more than all snares and nets, and by that same gate lions and wolves and tigers entered meekly with oxen and lambs.
Wesley states it in one line: the same hand that at first brought them to Adam to be named now brought them to Noah to be preserved.

Ellicott follows the same reckoning of the age and adds a detail easily missed — Shem was about a hundred and his brothers younger, and all three were married, though apparently as yet without children. He sets the story beside its Babylonian counterpart, where Xisuthrus takes aboard not only wild animals but seeds of every kind of plant, gold and silver, and slaves both male and female: there a whole tribe is saved with their chief, here one family only. On the seven days he passes on the Jewish tradition that they were the days of mourning for Methuselah, who died in the year of the flood.

11.pericope_label: The date, the fountains and the windows

schools.summary: Gill reads the six hundredth year as current, not complete, since Noah lived three hundred and fifty years after the flood and not fifty-one. Calvin frames the two causes by going back to the creation: the earth was originally covered with water, and by God's singular kindness the waters receded so that space might be left for living creatures — a thing philosophers must admit is contrary to nature, and which Scripture reckons among God's miracles. God raised for men a theatre in the habitable region of the earth, causing that the subterranean waters should not break out nor the celestial conspire with them; now those barriers were torn up. And here Calvin sets down the sentence that governs the passage: God might have deposited in veins of the earth as much water as human life required, but has designedly placed us between two graves, lest in fancied security we despise the kindness our life depends on — for the element philosophers count a principle of life threatens us with death from above and beneath, except so far as God's hand restrains it.

Henry sets the date at 1656 years from the creation and draws a note from the reckoning: the years of the old world are numbered not by the reigns of giants but by the lives of patriarchs, saints being of more account with God than princes. He and Wesley put the two causes in the language of storehouses — there needed no new creation of waters, God having laid up the deep in store and now broken it up, removing the mounds and fences set at the creation, so the sea returned to cover the earth as at first; while the rain that ordinarily descends in drops came down in streams, the bond of the thick clouds being loosed. Henry ends where the arithmetic began: God made the world in six days but was forty destroying it, for he is slow to anger; yet it came effectually.

Clarke reaches Gill's conclusion from the other end, counting the year in the ark and the death at nine hundred and fifty. He identifies the first month as Tisri and the second as Marcheshvan, the change of the year's beginning to Nisan having come only after the deliverance from Egypt; and he ventures a physical account, that an immense quantity of water occupied the centre of the antediluvian earth, so that as it burst forth the surrounding strata must have sunk to fill the vacuum — deriving the word rendered flood from a root meaning to confound. Wesley, with Henry, reckons the month about the beginning of November and notices the homely consequence that Noah had a harvest just before, to victual the ark.

Ellicott gives the reason for the autumn reckoning — the ecclesiastical year beginning in Abib commemorates the deliverance from Egypt and can have no place here — so the flood began toward the end of October and lasted till spring; and he proves the year lunar besides, the hundred and fifty days of prevailing running from the seventeenth of the second month to the seventeenth of the seventh, five months of thirty each. On the causes he is more cautious about the language and bolder about the event: the description is usually taken for extraordinary rain in the narrator's popular idiom, but the words suggest a great cosmic catastrophe by which some vast body of water was set loose — without which it is hard to see how the ark, a vessel incapable of sailing, could have gone against the current up to the watershed of Ararat. He adds that the earth's annual evaporation being fixed, its downpour concentrated into forty days would scarcely produce so vast a deluge.

12.pericope_label: Forty days of rain, and the Lord shut him in

schools.summary: Gill notes the door and the disposition of the creatures within. Calvin asks why the waters were not loosed at once and gives two reasons — partly for Noah, that by long meditation he might fix more deeply what he had learned by the word; partly for the wicked, that before dying they might feel the warnings they had derided were no empty threats. From this he draws an observation about ourselves: God so tempers his judgments that men may have leisure to consider them, but the depravity of our nature shows in this, that when his anger is poured out suddenly we are stupefied, and when it advances at a measured pace we grow so accustomed to it as to despise it. He defends the repetition that follows as deliberate, the Spirit meaning to hold our minds on a vengeance too terrible for language; and he turns to the carpentry at the end, finding it insufficient — that door must have been large which could admit an elephant, and no pitch tenacious enough to keep out the water through so many seams, so that Moses cuts off idle speculation by declaring the ark kept secure not by human artifice but by the secret power of God.

Henry hears in after his kind the language of the creation account, and takes it that just as many species were saved as created, and no more — but adds a warning, that when the occasion was over the restraint was lifted and the creatures were of the same kind as ever, for the ark did not alter their constitution; and hypocrites in the church, outwardly conforming to that ark's laws, may be as unchanged. On the shutting he gives two purposes: to secure Noah, the door shut close lest the waters break in and fast lest any break it down, so that God made him up as he makes up his jewels; and to exclude the rest, since hitherto the door had stood open and even in the last seven days a penitent might have been welcomed, whereas now God had shut it and none can open. His comparison is the finest thing here — God put Adam into paradise but did not shut him in, and Adam threw himself out; putting Noah into the ark he shut him in, so that when he brings a soul to Christ he secures its salvation, which is not in our keeping but in the Mediator's hand.

Wesley notes it rained without intermission or abatement, and on the whole earth at once. Clarke passes on Lightfoot's dating of the rain from the eighteenth of Marcheshvan to the twenty-eighth of Cisleu, and says more grimly that as God shut Noah in he shut the others out, having waited a hundred and twenty years on a generation that did not repent.

Ellicott finds the ascription remarkable, this act of personal care being assigned to Jehovah by name, whereas in the Chaldean Genesis the deity merely commands Xisuthrus to shut himself in. Keil, surveying what follows, calls the description simple and majestic, the almighty judgment of God set beside the love manifest within it.

17.pericope_label: The waters prevail, and the ark is lifted up

schools.summary: Gill traces the flight of those outside, from the lower rooms to the housetops, then to the tallest trees, then to the hills, and in vain. Calvin explains why Moses dwells on the totality: the design is that we should not ascribe to fortune the flood by which the world perished, however customary it is for men to veil the works of God; since it is plainly declared that whatever flourished was destroyed, we infer a signal and indisputable judgment — especially as Noah alone remained secure, having embraced by faith the word in which salvation was contained. Two opposites are joined, the whole race destroyed and one family safe, from which we learn how profitable it was for Noah to disregard the world and obey God alone, recorded not to praise the man but to invite our imitation. Peter makes the deliverance a figure of baptism and the Church is justly compared to the ark; but the likeness holds, Calvin insists, only because drawn from the word of God — and the Papists act ridiculously who fabricate an ark without the word.

Henry reads the temper of those watching the water rise: the profane world probably flattered themselves it would soon abate, but still it increased. When God judges he will overcome — if he begin, he will make an end; and there is warning in the slowness, since the gradual approaches of judgment, designed to bring sinners to repentance, are often abused instead to harden them. On the ark he gets two sentences worth the passage: the waters which broke down everything else bore up the ark, that which to unbelievers is a savour of death unto death being to the faithful a savour of life unto life; and the more the waters increased, the higher the ark rose toward heaven, so that sanctified afflictions are promotions. He then imagines the last hours outside — some climbing the trees and spinning out their terrors, some clinging to the ark and hoping that might be their safety which they had long made their sport, some pleading old acquaintance, to which the answer could only be that he had called and they refused, and that God had shut the door.

Wesley draws one dry inference: the mountains were covered, therefore mountains existed before the flood. Clarke meets the objection that there was not water enough by referring the doubter to Ray's Physico-theological Discourses.

Ellicott takes the fifteen cubits for a measurement rather than a flourish — the draught of the ark, computed after it settled near Ararat, some twenty-two feet, so that there must have been that depth even on the highest summit along its course. He doubts rain alone could account for it: taking England's mean annual rainfall of thirty inches and supposing the whole of it to fall every twenty-four hours, forty days would yield some hundred feet, enough to strip the mountains of soil and dig new courses for the rivers. But water seeks the lower ground throughout, so it is hard to see how it could stand twenty-two feet deep on the heights without some cosmic convulsion carrying the waters from the equator toward the poles — which would also remove the difficulty of the ark being borne against the current up into Armenia. Keil calls the whole description simple and majestic.

22.pericope_label: A hundred and fifty days, and how they are reckoned

schools.summary: Gill enters the caution that every living substance destroyed cannot mean literally everything, since trees survived — after the waters abated there was an olive tree from which the dove brought a leaf — so the sentence must be read of the animals. On the hundred and fifty days he reckons them not from the end of the forty days' rain but from the beginning of the flood, since from the seventeenth day of the second month to the seventeenth of the seventh is exactly five months. That leaves him the difficulty that the waters went on increasing after the rain had stopped, and he adopts Aben Ezra's solution, that there was continual rain afterwards though less vehement, since otherwise the increase is not easy to account for.

Clarke draws an inference from the phrase all that was in the dry land: only such animals as could not live in water were preserved in the ark. On the chronology he follows Lightfoot the other way, keeping the two sums distinct so that the forty days are not included in the hundred and fifty, and when the hundred and fifty were ended there were six months and ten days of the flood past.

Ellicott renders the phrase more exactly as everything that stood erect, and glosses the ground it was blotted from as the adamah, the portion subdued to his own use by the adam. On the reckoning he takes Gill's side and states it most clearly — the rains lasted forty days, for a hundred and ten more the waters still bore up the ark, and then it grounded. He alone reads the last verse for what it implies about the telling: the waters are said to have prevailed, which is literally that they were strong, and yet by that time they had abated, since instead of covering the hills to nearly four fathoms they had let the ark touch dry land. That shift suggests to him the personal experience of someone aboard, who would have known the water was still deep and powerful but would also have felt the vessel take the ground — the same argument he makes about the exactness of the dates, which tradition could have carried correctly only briefly before they had to be written down.
